bibliographic.title: Large language models propagate race-based medicine
bibliographic.authors: Jesutofunmi A. Omiye, Jenna C. Lester, Simon Spichak, Veronica Rotemberg, Roxana Daneshjou
bibliographic.citation_apa: Omiye, J. A., Lester, J. C., Spichak, S., Rotemberg, V., & Daneshjou, R. (2023). Large language models propagate race-based medicine. npj Digital Medicine, 6(1), 195. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41746-023-00939-z

methodology.method_family: comparative LLM prompt interrogation with repeated trials
methodology.study_design: expert-derived scenario questioning of four commercial LLMs, nine questions each interrogated five times (45 responses per model)
methodology.sample_description: four commercially available large language models assessed with medical race-based medicine and misconception scenarios
methodology.sample_size: 45 responses per model (nine questions x five repetitions x four models)
methodology.technology_context: commercially available LLMs queried with medically relevant questions; some models described as connecting to electronic health record systems; Bard noted as internet-accessible

eligibility.decision_rationale: The study provides primary empirical evidence that commercial LLMs in healthcare-oriented use can propagate harmful race-based medicine and show response inconsistency, supporting risk, bias, and harm themes in regulated LLM deployment. It does not examine conversational governance mechanisms such as guardrails, observability, human oversight, audit, compliance controls, or operational governance frameworks, so it is not central evidence for conversational governance.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front-matter text was supplied; full methods, complete model list, analysis procedures, limitations, and absence of governance framing should be verified before final inclusion.

appraisal.notes: Brief communication with a clearly stated objective and repeatable interrogation design. Provided excerpt lacks full methods, scoring rubric, statistical analysis, ethics discussion, and explicit limitations, limiting appraisal of rigor and transparency.

cerqual.explanation: Findings are coherent and adequately supported for the narrow claim that tested LLMs can output race-based medical misconceptions, but methodological detail is limited in the supplied text and the study's relevance to conversational governance is indirect.

coding.theme: LLM safety and bias in healthcare deployment
coding.subtheme: propagation of debunked race-based medical beliefs by commercial LLMs
rq_alignment: risk and harm in regulated LLM use
limited alignment with conversational governance controls

synthesis.main_claim: Four commercially available LLMs propagate harmful, inaccurate race-based medical content in response to expert-derived medical scenarios and are not always consistent across repeated identical questions.
synthesis.contribution: Empirical demonstration that LLMs proposed for healthcare and EHR-connected use can reproduce debunked racist medical ideas, highlighting deployment risk in a regulated domain.
synthesis.limitations: Supplied text does not report full model identification, complete analytic methods, formal bias measurement framework, governance interventions, or study limitations.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as supporting evidence on LLM bias, harm, and deployment risk in regulated healthcare contexts; not as central evidence on conversational governance architecture, oversight, or operational control mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Clear study objective focused on race-based medical content in LLMs
evidence.excerpt: The objective of this study is to assess whether four commercially available large language models (LLMs) propagate harmful, inaccurate, race-based content

evidence.claim: Empirical design with repeated questioning of multiple LLMs
evidence.excerpt: We assessed four large language models with nine different questions that were interrogated five times each with a total of 45 responses per model.

evidence.claim: All tested models showed harmful race-based outputs
evidence.excerpt: All models had examples of perpetuating race-based medicine in their responses.

evidence.claim: Response inconsistency across repeated identical prompts
evidence.excerpt: Models were not always consistent in their responses when asked the same question repeatedly.

evidence.claim: Healthcare regulated deployment context with potential harm
evidence.excerpt: LLMs are being proposed for use in the healthcare setting, with some models already connecting to electronic health record systems.

evidence.claim: Harm and debunked racist ideas as outcome risk
evidence.excerpt: these LLMs could potentially cause harm by perpetuating debunked, racist ideas.
The underlying training data used to build these models are not transparent

evidence.claim: Primary result that every LLM promoted race-based medicine or tropes
evidence.excerpt: every LLM model had instances of promoting race-based medicine/racist tropes or repeating unsub-stantiated claims around race

evidence.claim: Questions derived from physician expert input and prior misconception literature
evidence.excerpt: Questions were derived from discussions among four physician experts and prior work on race-based medical misconceptions believed by medical trainees.
this study assesses the potential of these models to regurgitate discredited, race-based medicine and debunked racist tropes.
